# Shepherd of Hermas Chapter 98 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Translator:** SOPHIA | **Source:** Codex Athous, Shepherd of Hermas 98 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-EC/SHE_098_page_001.jpg

---

## Similitude 9, Chapter 15

**1** "And the spotted stones — who are they?" **2** "These," he said, "are those who have believed and possess the greater part of their faith, but also have some share in the riches of this world; **3** when affliction comes, because of their wealth and pressing business affairs, these persons deny the Lord." **4** I said to him, "When then, Lord, will they be fit for the building of the tower?" **5** "When," he said, "the wealth that leads their souls astray has been cut away from them. **6** But if they repent first, they may be fit. For just as a round stone cannot become square unless it is cut and something removed from it, so those who are wealthy cannot be fit for the Lord unless something of their riches is taken from them." **7** "Understand this for yourself: when you were rich, you were useless; now you are useful and profitable for the life of God, because you have been made needy. Be useful to God — for even you yourself are taken from these same stones." **8** "And the other spotted stones — those with the white spots — who are they?" **9** "These are those who departed from God and blasphemed, and became betrayers of the servants of God. **10** For these there is no repentance but death; therefore they are black — for their kind is death." **11** "And those who gave back half-withered and cracked stones — who are they?" **12** "These are those who were always in harmony with one another and bore no grudge. They rejoiced greatly whenever they saw one another. **13** For this reason their stones were pulled partly from the tower; but because of their love for one another and their harmony, they were restored."

---

### Translator's Note
Verse 7 is one of the most personal moments in apocalyptic literature — the angel's direct pastoral address to Hermas, telling him that his own financial ruin is his spiritual making. The "betrayers of the servants of God" (v. 9) likely refers to Christians who informed on fellow believers to Roman authorities. SOPHIA follows LOGOS throughout; PNEUMA's "informers" in v. 9 is historically plausible but interpretive.
